_about: Baseline context for current wars and armed conflicts: who fights, why, and what is at stake. Durable facts only; who holds which town this week, casualty counts and the latest phase come from the system's own reports (conflict_context.py, 'where it stands now', cited and dated). Written into the repository and reviewed 2026-10-10; edit a copy in DATA_DIR/conflicts.json to correct it without a deploy. match_countries (when present) narrows which countries' reports count toward 'where it stands now' — a report anywhere in India is not about Kashmir; terms still match.

conflicts.name: Russia–Ukraine war
conflicts.sides_line: Russia vs Ukraine
conflicts.summary: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, eight years after it annexed Crimea and backed separatists in the Donbas. A largely attritional front runs through Kharkiv, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts; both sides strike deep with drones and missiles, Russia mainly at Ukraine's energy grid and cities, Ukraine at refineries, airbases and logistics inside Russia.

factions.name: Russian Armed Forces
factions.aims: Keep and extend the annexed Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts and Crimea; a neutral, disarmed Ukraine outside NATO.
factions.holds: Crimea, nearly all of Luhansk, most of Donetsk, much of Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts south and east of the Dnipro.

factions.name: Armed Forces of Ukraine
backers: European states and the EU (arms, finance)
factions.aims: Restore internationally recognised borders, or at least stop the advance with binding security guarantees.
factions.holds: The rest of Ukraine, including Kyiv, Kharkiv, Odesa, Dnipro and Zaporizhzhia city.

drivers: Moscow's claim to a sphere of influence and its opposition to Ukraine's turn to the EU and NATO
The unresolved 2014 annexation of Crimea and war in the Donbas
Competing claims about Ukrainian nationhood
stakes: European security and the credibility of NATO's eastern flank
Black Sea shipping and grain exports through Odesa
Energy: strikes on power grids and refineries, Russian oil revenue and the shadow tanker fleet
Nuclear safety at the occupied Zaporizhzhia plant

conflicts.name: Israel–Hamas war in Gaza
conflicts.sides_line: Israel vs Hamas
conflicts.summary: War since Hamas's attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, which killed about 1,200 people and took some 250 hostages. Israel's ground and air campaign has destroyed most of Gaza and displaced nearly all of its two million people; ceasefire arrangements have alternated with renewed fighting.

factions.name: Israel Defense Forces
factions.aims: Return of all hostages, destruction of Hamas's military and governing capacity, lasting security control over Gaza.
factions.holds: Security corridors and buffer zones inside Gaza; the extent changes with each phase.

factions.name: Hamas (Izz ad-Din al-Qassam Brigades)
factions.leader: Military and political leadership decimated since 2024; political bureau in Doha
factions.aims: Survive as an armed movement, secure Israeli withdrawal and prisoner releases, keep a role in Gaza's governance.
factions.holds: Underground networks and parts of Gaza not held by Israeli forces.

factions.name: Palestinian Islamic Jihad
factions.aims: Armed struggle against Israel; fights alongside Hamas.

drivers: Unresolved Israeli–Palestinian conflict: occupation, blockade, statehood
Hamas's armed rejection of Israel's existence
Israel's security doctrine after 7 October and the hostages
stakes: The remaining hostages and Palestinian prisoners
Famine and the humanitarian collapse in Gaza
Regional escalation through Hezbollah, the Houthis and Iran
Who governs and rebuilds Gaza; Saudi–Israeli normalisation

conflicts.name: Israel–Hezbollah conflict
conflicts.sides_line: Israel vs Hezbollah
conflicts.summary: Hezbollah opened a front in solidarity with Hamas the day after 7 October; in autumn 2024 Israel escalated, killed Hassan Nasrallah and most of the group's command, and invaded southern Lebanon. A ceasefire from 27 November 2024 requires Hezbollah to leave the area south of the Litani; Israel keeps positions on the border and continues strikes it says target rearmament.

factions.name: Israel Defense Forces
factions.aims: Disarm Hezbollah at least south of the Litani so northern Israel's residents can stay home.
factions.holds: Several hilltop positions inside southern Lebanon.

factions.name: Hezbollah
backers: Iran (funding, missiles; supply route through Syria cut since Assad's fall)
factions.aims: Keep its weapons and its place in Lebanese politics.
factions.holds: Political and social control across much of the south, the Bekaa and Beirut's southern suburbs.

factions.name: Lebanese Armed Forces
factions.aims: Deploy south of the Litani and bring all weapons under state control.
factions.holds: Deploying in the south under the ceasefire mechanism.

drivers: Hezbollah's role in Iran's regional alliance
Israel's demand for a disarmed border
A Lebanese state too weak to monopolise force
stakes: Displacement on both sides of the border

conflicts.name: War in Yemen and the Red Sea
conflicts.sides_line: Houthis vs the government and its allies
conflicts.summary: The Houthi movement took Sanaa in 2014; a Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015. Front lines have been largely frozen since a 2022 truce, while the Houthis attack shipping in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden and fire at Israel, drawing US and Israeli strikes. The anti-Houthi camp is itself split between the government and southern separatists.

factions.name: Ansar Allah (Houthis)
factions.aims: Rule Yemen; press Israel and its supporters through the Red Sea.
factions.holds: Sanaa, Hodeidah and most of the populous north-west.

factions.name: Presidential Leadership Council and government forces
factions.aims: Restore the internationally recognised government.
factions.holds: Marib, parts of Taiz, the east; seat in Aden.

factions.name: Southern Transitional Council
factions.aims: An independent South Yemen.
factions.holds: Aden and much of the south.

factions.name: National Resistance and Giants Brigades
factions.aims: Hold the Red Sea coast from Bab el-Mandeb to Hodeidah's edge.
factions.holds: Mokha, Dhubab and the west coast south of Hodeidah.

factions.name: Al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula
factions.aims: Insurgency against all sides.
factions.holds: Pockets in Abyan and Shabwa.

drivers: The Houthi seizure of the state
Saudi–Iranian rivalry
Southern grievances and the push for secession
A divided central bank and economy
stakes: Shipping through Bab el-Mandeb and the Suez route
One of the world's worst humanitarian crises
US and Israeli strikes and the risk of wider war with Iran

conflicts.name: Sudan civil war
conflicts.sides_line: SAF vs RSF
conflicts.summary: A war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, former partners in the 2021 coup, over who controls the state and its army. The army retook Khartoum in 2025 and governs from Port Sudan; the RSF dominates Darfur and parts of Kordofan and has set up a rival administration. Mass killings along ethnic lines, especially in Darfur.

factions.name: Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF)
factions.aims: Defeat or absorb the RSF and keep the army at the centre of the state.
factions.holds: The north, east and centre, Khartoum, Port Sudan.

factions.name: Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
backers: Supply routes through Chad, Libya and the Central African Republic
factions.aims: Power for itself and its allies; a rival government in the west.
factions.holds: Most of Darfur and parts of Kordofan.

factions.name: Allied armed movements
factions.aims: Darfuri movements (Joint Forces) defending their communities, mostly alongside the army.
factions.holds: Parts of North Darfur.

drivers: A power struggle between Burhan and Hemedti over integrating the RSF into the army
Gold and other resources financing both sides
The unresolved legacy of Darfur and the 2019 revolution
stakes: The world's largest displacement crisis and famine
Red Sea access and foreign naval bases
Proxy competition between the UAE, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Turkey

conflicts.name: Central Sahel insurgency (Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger)
conflicts.sides_line: Juntas and Russia vs JNIM and Islamic State
conflicts.summary: Jihadist insurgencies that began in northern Mali in 2012 have spread across Mali, Burkina Faso and western Niger. Military juntas that took power between 2020 and 2023 expelled French and UN forces, left ECOWAS, formed the Alliance of Sahel States and turned to Russia. The al-Qaeda-linked JNIM blockades roads and towns; massacres of civilians by all sides are frequent.

factions.name: Alliance of Sahel States juntas
factions.leader: Assimi Goïta (Mali), Ibrahim Traoré (Burkina Faso), Abdourahamane Tiani (Niger)
factions.aims: Regime survival and military victory; sovereignty from France and ECOWAS.
factions.holds: Capitals and garrison towns; large rural areas contested.

factions.name: JNIM (Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin)
factions.aims: Islamic governance across the Sahel; strangle the juntas economically.
factions.holds: Wide rural areas of central and northern Mali and much of Burkina Faso.

factions.name: Islamic State Sahel Province
factions.aims: A caliphate province in the tri-border area.
factions.holds: Ménaka and the Mali–Niger–Burkina tri-border area.

factions.name: Azawad Liberation Front (FLA)
factions.aims: Autonomy or independence for northern Mali (Azawad).
factions.holds: Parts of the Kidal region and the north.

drivers: Absent or abusive states in the periphery
Communal conflict between herders and farmers, and ethnic profiling of Fulani
Coups and the break with France, the UN and ECOWAS
stakes: Spread toward coastal states: Benin, Togo, Ghana, Côte d'Ivoire
Fuel and food blockades of cities
Gold mines and Russia's foothold in Africa

conflicts.name: War in eastern DR Congo
conflicts.sides_line: M23/AFC (Rwanda-backed) vs Congo's army and allies
conflicts.summary: The M23 rebellion, revived in late 2021 with Rwandan troops and weapons according to UN experts, took Goma and Bukavu in early 2025 and runs a parallel administration in North and South Kivu. US- and Qatar-brokered agreements have not ended the fighting; dozens of other armed groups, including the IS-linked ADF, kill civilians across the east.

factions.name: M23 / Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC)
factions.aims: Control of the Kivus and a say in Kinshasa; protection of Congolese Tutsi.
factions.holds: Goma, Bukavu and large parts of North and South Kivu.

factions.name: Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) and allies
factions.aims: Recover the territory and remove Rwandan influence.
factions.holds: Most of the rest of the east; front lines around the Kivus.

factions.name: Allied Democratic Forces (ADF)
factions.aims: Insurgency; massacres of civilians in North Kivu and Ituri.
factions.holds: Forests around Beni and in Ituri.

drivers: Rwanda's security claims about the FDLR and its economic interests
Control of minerals: coltan, gold, tin
Land, citizenship and ethnic tensions in the Kivus
stakes: A regional war drawing in Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda

conflicts.name: Al-Shabaab insurgency in Somalia
conflicts.sides_line: Federal government and AU vs al-Shabaab
conflicts.summary: Al-Qaeda's Somali affiliate controls much of the rural south and centre and regularly attacks Mogadishu. The federal government, supported by an African Union mission, US air strikes and Turkey, has regained and lost ground; disputes with federal member states such as Jubaland and Puntland weaken the effort. An Islamic State branch is based in Puntland's mountains.

factions.name: Federal Government of Somalia
factions.aims: Defeat al-Shabaab and consolidate a federal state.
factions.holds: Mogadishu and major towns.

factions.name: Al-Shabaab
factions.aims: An Islamic state across Somalia.
factions.holds: Much of rural Middle and Lower Shabelle, Jubba valley and central regions.

factions.name: Islamic State Somalia
factions.aims: A base for the Islamic State's African operations.
factions.holds: Cal Miskaad mountains in Puntland, under Puntland offensive.

drivers: State collapse since 1991 and clan politics
Federal–regional disputes
Al-Shabaab's taxation and shadow governance
stakes: Gulf of Aden shipping and a revival of piracy

conflicts.name: Insurgencies in Ethiopia (Amhara, Oromia) and the Eritrea tension
conflicts.sides_line: Federal government vs Fano and OLA
conflicts.summary: After the 2020–2022 Tigray war, Amhara's Fano militias rose against the federal army in 2023 and the Oromo Liberation Army fights in Oromia. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's talk of Red Sea access raises fears of war with Eritrea, which is close to factions in Tigray.

factions.name: Ethiopian National Defense Force
factions.aims: Disarm regional forces and keep federal authority.
factions.holds: Cities and main roads.

factions.name: Fano militias
factions.aims: Defend Amhara interests; oppose Abiy's government.
factions.holds: Much of rural Amhara.

factions.name: Oromo Liberation Army
factions.aims: Self-determination for Oromia.
factions.holds: Rural western and southern Oromia.

drivers: Ethnic federalism and disputed territories
Disarmament of regional special forces after the Tigray war
Abiy's push for sea access
stakes: The Horn of Africa's balance and the Red Sea

conflicts.name: Myanmar civil war
conflicts.sides_line: Military junta vs resistance and ethnic armies
conflicts.summary: Since the 2021 coup, the military has fought pro-democracy People's Defence Forces and long-standing ethnic armed organisations, which made large gains from late 2023. The army retains the centre and the cities, relies on air strikes, and held elections in late 2025 that the opposition rejected.

factions.name: Myanmar military (State Administration Council and its successor)
factions.aims: Keep power and Myanmar's unity under military control.
factions.holds: Naypyidaw, Yangon, Mandalay and the central plains.

factions.name: Arakan Army
factions.aims: Self-rule in Rakhine.
factions.holds: Most of Rakhine State.

factions.name: Kachin Independence Army and northern armies (TNLA, MNDAA)
factions.aims: Autonomy; control of borders and resources.
factions.holds: Large areas of Kachin and northern Shan, varying under Chinese pressure.

factions.name: National Unity Government and People's Defence Forces
factions.aims: End military rule; a federal democracy.
factions.holds: Rural areas of Sagaing, Magway and elsewhere.

drivers: The 2021 coup
Decades of ethnic armed struggle for autonomy
Control of jade, rare earths and border trade
stakes: China's corridor and the Kyaukphyu port
The Rohingya and refugees in Bangladesh
Scam compounds and narcotics on the borders

conflicts.name: Syria after Assad
conflicts.sides_line: Transitional government vs rivals, with Israel and Turkey involved
conflicts.summary: Rebels led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham ended Bashar al-Assad's rule in December 2024 after thirteen years of civil war. Ahmed al-Sharaa leads a transitional government seeking sanctions relief and recognition; violence against Alawites on the coast and Druze in Sweida, an unsettled deal with the Kurdish-led SDF, Israeli strikes and an Israeli buffer zone in the south, and Islamic State remnants test it.

factions.name: Transitional government and its army
factions.aims: One state and one army; recognition and reconstruction.
factions.holds: Damascus, Aleppo, Homs, Hama, Idlib and the coast.

factions.name: Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF)
factions.aims: Keep self-rule in the north-east within an agreed integration.
factions.holds: The north-east east of the Euphrates, oil fields, IS detention camps.

factions.name: Israel
factions.aims: A demilitarised south and protection it claims for the Druze.
factions.holds: A buffer zone beyond the Golan line, including Mount Hermon.

factions.name: Islamic State remnants
factions.aims: Insurgency.
factions.holds: Cells in the central desert.

drivers: The legacy of the civil war and sectarian revenge
Kurdish autonomy against centralisation
Israeli and Turkish security agendas
stakes: Russia's bases at Hmeimim and Tartus
IS detainees and families in al-Hol

conflicts.name: Israel–Iran confrontation
conflicts.sides_line: Israel (and the US) vs Iran
conflicts.summary: Decades of shadow war became direct exchanges in 2024. In June 2025 Israel struck Iran's nuclear sites, air defences and commanders for twelve days, the United States bombed Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan, and Iran answered with missile barrages before a ceasefire. UN sanctions were reimposed in September 2025; Iran's nuclear material and its cooperation with inspectors remain disputed.

factions.name: Israel
factions.aims: Prevent an Iranian nuclear weapon; weaken Iran's regional network.

factions.name: Islamic Republic of Iran (IRGC)
factions.aims: Regime survival, deterrence, keep enrichment.

drivers: Iran's nuclear programme
Iran's support for Hezbollah, the Houthis and Iraqi militias
Israel's doctrine of pre-emption
stakes: Nuclear proliferation in the Middle East
Oil through the Strait of Hormuz

conflicts.name: Gang war in Haiti
conflicts.sides_line: Gang coalition vs police and international force
conflicts.summary: Since President Jovenel Moïse's assassination in 2021, gang coalitions have taken most of Port-au-Prince and pushed into the Artibonite. A Kenya-led mission did not turn the tide; a UN-authorised force was approved in 2025 to replace it. More than a million people are displaced.

factions.name: Viv Ansanm gang coalition
backers: Arms trafficked from the United States
factions.aims: Territory, extortion and a political role.
factions.holds: Most of Port-au-Prince and main roads out of it.

factions.name: Haitian National Police and the international force
factions.aims: Retake the capital and hold elections.
factions.holds: Parts of the capital and other cities.

drivers: State collapse and elite capture
Weapons trafficking
Poverty and the absence of an elected government

conflicts.name: Nigeria's insurgencies and banditry
conflicts.sides_line: Nigerian forces vs ISWAP, Boko Haram and bandits
conflicts.summary: Jihadists of Islamic State West Africa Province and Boko Haram (JAS) fight in the north-east around Lake Chad; armed bandit gangs raid and kidnap across the north-west; farmer–herder and communal killings recur in the Middle Belt.

factions.name: Nigerian Armed Forces
backers: Multinational Joint Task Force (Lake Chad states)
factions.aims: Contain the insurgencies and banditry.
factions.holds: Cities and garrisons.

factions.name: Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP)
factions.aims: Governance around Lake Chad.
factions.holds: Lake Chad islands and parts of Borno.

factions.name: Boko Haram (JAS)
factions.aims: Insurgency.
factions.holds: Sambisa forest and the Mandara mountains.

factions.name: Bandit groups
factions.aims: Ransom, cattle and control of villages.
factions.holds: Rural Zamfara, Katsina, Sokoto, Kaduna.

drivers: Poverty, land and climate pressure
Weak rural policing
Jihadist ideology and the Lake Chad economy
stakes: Spill-over into Niger, Chad and Cameroon

conflicts.name: Insurgency in Cabo Delgado
conflicts.sides_line: Mozambique and Rwanda vs Islamic State Mozambique
conflicts.summary: An Islamic State-affiliated insurgency in Mozambique's northern province, near one of Africa's largest gas projects. Rwandan troops secure the gas area; attacks continue in the districts around it.

factions.name: Mozambican forces with Rwandan troops
factions.aims: Secure the province and the LNG project.
factions.holds: Palma, Mocímboa da Praia and the gas peninsula.

factions.name: Islamic State Mozambique
factions.aims: Insurgency in Cabo Delgado and Niassa.
factions.holds: Mobile across rural districts.

drivers: Marginalisation of the north and its youth
Resource wealth that bypasses locals

conflicts.name: Libya's divided state
conflicts.sides_line: Tripoli government vs Haftar's east
conflicts.summary: Libya has had rival authorities since 2014: a UN-recognised government in Tripoli and Khalifa Haftar's forces controlling the east and south. Open war ended in 2020, but militias clash in Tripoli and foreign forces remain.

factions.name: Government of National Unity and Tripoli militias
factions.aims: Keep power in the west.
factions.holds: Tripoli and the north-west.

factions.name: Libyan National Army
factions.aims: Rule all Libya.
factions.holds: Benghazi, the east, the south and most oil fields.

drivers: Control of oil revenue and the central bank
Rival legitimacies since 2014
Foreign patrons
stakes: Russia's base network toward the Sahel and Sudan

conflicts.name: Pakistan's insurgencies and the Afghan border
conflicts.sides_line: Pakistan vs TTP and Baloch separatists
conflicts.summary: The Pakistani Taliban (TTP), sheltered in Afghanistan, wage a growing insurgency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa; Baloch separatists, chiefly the BLA, attack security forces, Chinese projects and trains in Balochistan. Pakistan has struck inside Afghanistan and clashed with Taliban forces on the border.

factions.name: Pakistan Army and security forces
factions.aims: Defeat the TTP and separatists; force Kabul to act.

factions.name: Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP)
factions.aims: Islamic rule in the tribal areas.
factions.holds: Influence in parts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

factions.name: Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA)
factions.aims: Independence for Balochistan.

drivers: The Afghan Taliban's return in 2021
Baloch grievances over resources and repression
Militancy along the Durand Line
stakes: The China–Pakistan Economic Corridor and Gwadar

conflicts.name: India–Pakistan rivalry over Kashmir
conflicts.sides_line: India vs Pakistan
conflicts.summary: Nuclear-armed neighbours divided by the Line of Control in Kashmir. After a militant attack on tourists at Pahalgam in April 2025, India struck targets in Pakistan in May and the two exchanged missile, drone and artillery fire for four days before a ceasefire; India suspended the Indus Waters Treaty.

factions.name: India
factions.aims: End cross-border militancy; full control of Jammu and Kashmir.
factions.holds: Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh.

factions.name: Pakistan
factions.aims: Kashmir's status settled in its favour; deter India.
factions.holds: Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan.

drivers: The unresolved partition of Kashmir
Militant groups based in Pakistan
Water: the Indus Waters Treaty

conflicts.name: Colombia's armed conflict
conflicts.sides_line: State vs ELN, FARC dissidents and the Clan del Golfo
conflicts.summary: Despite the 2016 FARC peace deal, the ELN guerrilla, FARC dissident factions and the Clan del Golfo fight the state and each other over coca, mining and smuggling routes. Fighting in Catatumbo in 2025 displaced tens of thousands.

factions.name: Colombian military and police
factions.aims: Retake territory; negotiate where possible.

factions.name: ELN
factions.aims: Political and territorial control.
factions.holds: Catatumbo, Arauca, Chocó border areas.

factions.name: FARC dissidents (EMC and others)
factions.aims: Control of coca regions.
factions.holds: Cauca, Guaviare, Caquetá.

factions.name: Clan del Golfo (EGC)
factions.aims: Cocaine routes to the Caribbean.
factions.holds: Urabá and the north-west.

drivers: Cocaine and illegal mining profits
State absence in the periphery
Unfinished peace processes

conflicts.name: Mexico's cartel wars
conflicts.sides_line: Cartels vs each other and the state
conflicts.summary: Cartels fight each other and the security forces; since September 2024 the Sinaloa Cartel has been at war with itself between the Chapitos and the Mayo Zambada faction, centred on Culiacán. The United States designated major cartels as terrorist organisations in 2025 and presses Mexico over fentanyl.

factions.name: Mexican Army, National Guard and police
factions.aims: Reduce violence and fentanyl trafficking; avoid US unilateral action.

factions.name: Sinaloa Cartel (Chapitos vs Mayos)
factions.aims: Control of Sinaloa and of trafficking routes.
factions.holds: Sinaloa and parts of the north-west.

factions.name: Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG)
factions.aims: National dominance.
factions.holds: Jalisco and many states.

drivers: US demand for drugs and the flow of US guns south
Fragmentation of cartels
Corruption

conflicts.name: Anglophone crisis in Cameroon
conflicts.sides_line: Cameroon's army vs Ambazonian separatists
conflicts.summary: Separatists in Cameroon's two English-speaking regions declared 'Ambazonia' in 2017 after crackdowns on protests; fighting with the army, abductions and school closures continue. Boko Haram and ISWAP also attack in the Far North.

factions.name: Cameroonian Armed Forces
factions.aims: Crush the separatists.
factions.holds: Towns.

factions.name: Ambazonian separatist groups
factions.aims: Independence for the Northwest and Southwest regions.
factions.holds: Rural areas of the two regions.

drivers: Marginalisation of the anglophone minority
Repression of 2016 protests

conflicts.name: South Sudan's fraying peace
conflicts.sides_line: Kiir's government vs Machar's SPLM-IO and militias
conflicts.summary: The 2018 deal that ended the civil war between President Salva Kiir and Riek Machar is unravelling: fighting with the White Army around Nasir in 2025 led to Machar's arrest, and Ugandan troops deployed to back Kiir.

factions.name: SSPDF and government
factions.aims: Keep power; manage succession.
factions.holds: Juba and most towns.

factions.name: SPLM-IO and allied militias (White Army)
factions.aims: Power-sharing and protection of Nuer communities.
factions.holds: Parts of Upper Nile and Jonglei.

drivers: Elite rivalry between Kiir and Machar
Ethnic mobilisation (Dinka, Nuer)
Oil revenue
stakes: Oil exports through Sudan, disrupted by Sudan's war
